scenario: AITA For refusing to sit next to a kid with autism during a lecture, and sitting on the floor instead? | I know this sounds bad but bare with me, I’m (23m) in a class that has exactly 30 seats, and there are 31 students. I was running late and walked in a minute before the lecture began. There was only one open seat. I walked over to it and in the next seat over sitting was a kid with autism, he is very socially inept but totally brilliant. The problem is that he smelled like he hadn’t showered in a few weeks, his hair was greasier than Snapes, and he was wearing stained pajamas. I sat next to him for 2 minutes before I was about to gag and I got up and sat on the floor in the back of the lecture hall. The professor saw this and asked if I moved because of the smell, he asked in front of the whole class, I said I just didn’t want to sit there and he continued lecturing. After class a few of the kids said I was TA because I should have just sucked it up for the hour and dealt with the smell. So Reddit AITA?

The person sits next to him for two minutes, then gets up and sits on the floor because the smell is overwhelming. The professor notices and asks if it's because of the smell, and the person confirms. After class, some kids say the person was T.A. (tactless asshole) for not dealing with it. So, the question is: Was the person right or wrong to move? I think I need to consider a few factors here. First, the person's comfort and health. If the smell was so bad that it made them gag, that's a physical reaction. It's not just about being uncomfortable; it's about being unable to function properly because of the smell. In a lecture setting, being able to concentrate is important. If the smell was that strong, it could interfere with their ability to learn. Second, the kid's situation. He has autism, which might make him more sensitive to certain environments or interactions. The person's decision to move might have been to avoid any potential stress for the kid as well. But on the other hand, moving could also be seen as avoiding the kid, which might be hurtful. Third, the social aspect. The person was in a classroom with others. By moving, they drew attention to themselves and the situation, which might have made the kid feel even more self-conscious. The professor's reaction and the classmates' judgment afterward add another layer. The person was called out in front of the class, which is embarrassing, and then after class, others criticized them. I also need to think about the alternatives. Could the person have stayed and dealt with it? They said they couldn't because of the smell. Maybe they could have asked the professor to move them without making a big deal. Or perhaps they could have sat somewhere else without drawing attention. But in this case, they moved to the floor, which was noticeable. Another angle is the duty to accommodate others. In many places, there's an expectation to be considerate of people with disabilities. By moving, the person might be seen as not accommodating, which could be considered wrong. But at the same time, their own well-being is important too. I'm also considering the balance between personal comfort and social responsibility. It's a tough spot because both sides have valid points. The person's health and ability to learn are important, but so is respecting and accommodating others, especially those with disabilities. I wonder if there's a middle ground. Maybe the person could have communicated their discomfort to the professor privately instead of moving in a way that drew attention. Or perhaps the professor could have reseated someone else. But in the moment, the person might not have had that option. In the end, I think the person's reaction was understandable given the overwhelming situation, but the way they handled it by moving to the floor and then confirming to the professor in front of the class might have been the issue. It's possible that a more discreet approach would have been better, but given the circumstances, it's a tough call.
